annotations.keyFindings: Decay-affected surfaces rose by 0.7 per child five years after cessation in one city with no change in the comparison city; largest increase in children eligible for free school meals.
annotations.limitations: Two cities with different dental services; examiners not blinded.

annotations.keyFindings: Among 36 residents, councillors and professionals, views were shaped more by trust than by evidence about teeth; opponents framed choice, supporters fairness.
annotations.limitations: Parents of young children under-represented; English-language interviews only.

annotations.keyFindings: Only 38 percent of 1,212 parents knew whether their water was fluoridated, lowest in the most deprived areas; knowing did not change toothpaste use.
annotations.limitations: Lower response in deprived areas; self-report.

annotations.keyFindings: The 22 dentists and dental nurses increased varnish but could not reach non-attending families and felt left to explain the decision.
Extractions under general anaesthesia rose most in the most deprived quintile (rate ratio 1.46) and little in the least deprived (rate ratio 1.05).
annotations.limitations: Concurrent referral pathway change; extractions are a late outcome.

annotations.keyFindings: Of 1,960 consultation responses, 42 percent cited unsupported health fears and 27 percent questioned the council's honesty; parents of young children rarely responded.
Across 31 studies, deliberative methods reached a broader range of residents than open consultations dominated by organised groups.
annotations.limitations: Few evaluations of effects on trust; low-literacy groups rarely reached.

claims.text: In one city that stopped fluoridation, decay-affected surfaces in children rose by 0.7 per child over five years, with no change in the comparison city.
claims.passage: Decay-affected surfaces rose by 0.7 per child in the city that stopped, with no change in the comparison city.
claims.interpretation: A plausible local harm; it frames but does not answer the local question.

claims.text: After fluoridation ended in one region, extractions under general anaesthesia rose most in the most deprived quintile (rate ratio 1.46).

claims.interpretation: Any harm is likely to fall on families with the least access to dental care.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Comparative studies suggest that decay and extractions rise after fluoridation stops, most in deprived children, though confounded by service changes. Qualitative and consultation studies show that views are driven by trust and framed as choice against fairness, that many parents do not know their fluoridation status, and that open consultations are dominated by organised groups while parents of young children and deprived families are rarely heard. Dental teams feel left to explain the decision. No retrieved study reports the views of families after cessation in their own words.
gradeRationale: Observational comparisons with confounding for outcomes; single-site qualitative and content analyses for views; consistent themes but limited transferability.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five source-derived claims; overall certainty low.
